prs.title: Add experimental Automatic agent execution
prs.body:
## Summary

Add a platform-wide **Automatic Agent Execution** experiment under Settings → AI → Behavior. It is off by default: existing installations retain Delegated execution. Operators can opt in without replacing agents, tools, permissions, entry points or worker infrastructure.

- **Delegated:** the entry agent uses its tools and reaches specialists through isolated child runs.
- **Automatic:** the owner loads approved specialist instructions, discovers individual tools and calls them in the same conversation. It can still choose an isolated subagent.

Both use the standard Pydantic AI loop. Automatic uses native deferred capabilities, keyword ToolSearch and Harness SubAgents, backed by Bifrost's existing executors and live authorization of the caller, rooted approved agent paths, source schemas and workflow bindings. No new registry, worker service, retry service or per-session container.

The settings update preserves unrelated chat instructions, including concurrent independent changes. Each owning run retains its selected mode through child execution and resumption; summarization cannot choose or discard it. Chat and autonomous execution share the policy. Existing direct MCP tool calls remain driven by the external client; Bifrost runs launched through MCP follow the platform setting.

Failed workflow calls also retain actionable returned execution details and partial receipts. Existing timeout/child lifecycle paths are reused. Mapping diagnosis #1016 and instance finalization repairs are separate. Refs #1015 and #1014.

## Evidence and limitations

The previous frozen 96-run comparison tied 35/48 successful tasks per arrangement. Automatic used fewer model/child calls in aggregate, but this does **not establish better ticket completion**. The legacy arm was its delegation surface emulated on the same SDK, not an old worker binary. Detailed cohorts and limitations are retained in #1015; they are not pooled with newer checks.

The rollout separately audits all 62 active production agent definitions and proposes 11 narrow instruction replacements across 9 loose agents. It preserves confirmation, exact resource authority, business admission/finalization and result contracts. Solution-managed independent-review boundaries remain unchanged. Those private instance edits are not part of this public source patch and will only be applied after deployment.

Seven additional Sonnet 5.5 first-decision checks exercise direct discovery, the Delegated control, intermediate findings, script confirmation, missing scope, an on-premises authority boundary and Triage admission. These are routing checks without executed tools, not a full-loop or production-default-model accuracy benchmark.

prs.title: Resolve App slugs across the caller's reach
prs.body:
## Product Updates

- [ ] Highlight
- [x] Other: Platform admins can again refresh, deep-link and stay on an App that belongs to a client organization.
- [ ] Omit

Disposition: `product-updates/dispositions/pr-1029.json` (`other`, `category: fix`).

## Summary

**Symptom.** A Platform Admin (home org = provider org) gets `404 Application '<slug>' not found` from `GET /api/applications/{slug}` for every App that belongs to a client org, while `GET /api/applications` lists those Apps and the ID path (`/api/applications/{id}/draft`) returns 200. In the browser:
- **Refresh or deep link:** `/apps/<slug>` or `/apps/<slug>/preview/...` shows "Couldn't open this application" (`RouteLoadError`).
- **Clicking in from the apps page:** this works, because the list prefetch seeds the detail cache (`detail-route-loaders.ts:62`) and the route loader never calls the server.
- **Mid-session:** once that cache goes stale (60 s), any focus or reconnect refetch replaces the open App with "App could not be loaded" (`AppRouter.tsx:77`).

Reproduced on a production instance against 7 client-org Apps (404) and several provider-org Apps (200).

**Root cause.** #996 removed the Platform Admin branch that resolved slugs with `get_by_slug_global`. The slug now goes through `OrgScopedRepository.get`'s name cascade, which queries only `shared_read_organization(caller, None)`, the caller's home org, and then global. A row in another org is never considered, so the access decision is never reached. `is_superuser` is forced to `False` in Caller mode, so admins get the same cascade. The unit test `test_superuser_resolves_cross_org_slug` mocks `_application_repository`, so nothing caught it.

**Fix.**
- **Cross-org slug lookup:** in Caller mode, `ApplicationRepository.get` resolves slug lookups with `_get_by_slug_for_caller`. It selects every App with that slug, keeping the `solution_id IS NULL` filter unless `include_solution_managed`. It then admits each row with `_can_access_entity`, the same complete decision ID reads and `filter_readable` use. That decision runs on the row's real org, so reach, named permission, sharing, external-user and embed rules all still apply. No row becomes reachable that the ID path didn't already admit.
- **Shared slugs:** `_repo` App slugs are globally unique. Solution installs may share a slug across orgs. When several rows are readable, the order is: the selected org, then the home org, then global, then a stable pick by `id`. This matches the pre-#996 `get_by_slug_global` tiebreak.
- **`get_by_slug_global` stays.** It is still the slug-collision guard on create and rename. Its docstring and two stale test comments are updated.

**Known limitation (pre-existing, not a regression).** The slug route doesn't accept a scope hint. So if an admin's reach covers two orgs that each install the same Solution, only one of them opens by slug: home org, then global, then lowest id. Pre-#996 behaved the same. A follow-up could accept `?scope=` on `GET /{slug}` the way the list does.

## Validation

- New e2e test `tests/e2e/api/test_resource_access.py::test_cross_org_app_opens_by_slug_within_reach`: the Platform Admin and the owning org's user get 200, and another org's user gets 404. It **fails on `main`** with the 404 and passes with the fix.
- New unit tests `tests/unit/repositories/test_application_slug_for_caller.py`:
  - a readable cross-org row resolves and an unreadable one stays hidden;
  - the preference order;
  - an unreadable preferred row doesn't block a readable one;
  - Solution-managed rows are excluded unless requested, and the WHERE clause has no org filter.

  - `./test.sh tests/e2e/api/test_app*.py -q` → 36 passed

prs.title: Host platform control in the API lifecycle (opt-in, #769 stage 1)
prs.body:
## Product Updates

- [ ] Highlight
- [ ] Other
- [x] Omit — opt-in deployment infrastructure. Default installations keep control in the scheduler; the only visible change is that Diagnostics → Scheduler now also lists the existing every-minute logo-thumbnail backfill, which previously ran unlisted.

## Summary

Stage 1 of the API-owned unified runtime (#769, handoff in #1030). Platform control (scheduled-trigger leadership and Kubernetes build reconciliation) is extracted from the scheduler into a shared `ControlPlane` (`api/src/scheduler/control.py`). `BIFROST_CONTROL_PLANE_HOST` chooses the host:

- `scheduler` (default): unchanged. Scheduler replicas host control and execute local platform jobs.
- `api`: every API replica hosts control in its lifespan, joining after the schema gate without delaying HTTP startup. Scheduler replicas only execute local platform jobs. API replicas never run platform-job handlers. Existing workflow, agent and platform-job execution is untouched.

**Ownership and fencing**
- Both hosts compete for the same `scheduler-triggers` lease. An old scheduler and a new API replica therefore never lead together during a switch or mixed-version rollout.
- The leader keeps a conservative local lease deadline, measured from before each acquire/renew request, minus a drift margin. A renewal is bounded by that deadline, and every scheduled callback re-checks it before starting. A partitioned leader stops producing triggers before PostgreSQL can elect a successor.
- A new leader staggers its run-at-startup callbacks 0.5 s apart instead of firing ~16 at once. Recurring runs are not throttled: a throttled run would count as a running instance, and APScheduler would skip its next firing.
- API-hosted control is supervised. If startup fails (schema gate, database outage) or a control loop exits, that replica releases the lease and restarts control after 30 s. HTTP keeps serving.
- Shutdown cancels a pending schema-gate wait and returns only once the lease is released, so the database stays open until then.

**Catalog**
- `registry.py` is now the single declarative source for what a leader installs and what Diagnostics lists. The legacy schedule set (ids, triggers, startup runs) is pinned by test.
- Triggers are explicitly UTC.
- The previously hidden logo-thumbnail backfill is now listed.

**Schedule occurrences across failover** (migration `20261022_schedule_occurrences`)
- `events.occurrence_key` has a partial unique index, built `CONCURRENTLY`, so overlapping leaders fire an occurrence at most once.
- `scheduler_task_states.cursor_at` extends each scan back to the last successful scan, capped at 10 minutes. A successor fires an occurrence missed during failover once. The one-minute floor keeps today's skip-on-overlap semantics.
- Occurrences are keyed in UTC, so DST-repeated wall-clock times stay distinct.
- An unkeyed event at the same instant, written by an older image during a rollout or rollback, also counts as fired.
- Diagnostics capacity counts only replicas that execute platform jobs. API control replicas appear in the replica list with zero slots.

**Deployment**
- Compose: `BIFROST_CONTROL_PLANE_HOST` added to api/scheduler.
- New opt-in overlay `deploy/kubernetes/api-control`, layered on `builds`. It moves the Job-controller ServiceAccount to the API and removes it from the scheduler.
- Kind: `BIFROST_KIND_API_CONTROL=1` (two API replicas) and `./test.sh kubernetes control-experiment`.

## Evidence

**Live Kind runs** (two API replicas hosting control, scheduler executing jobs only, build Jobs enabled; `./test.sh kubernetes control-experiment`):

| Check | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Election | One API pod holds the lease. Both API replicas report 0 slots; the scheduler reports 2 slots. |
| Steady state | Every run in the window came from the leader. No `schedule_processor` minute ran twice. |
| Leader process SIGKILLed on the node (no shutdown hooks) | Successor took over at DB expiry: 23.9 s, and 25.0 s after the review fixes. No interleaved owners, no duplicate minutes. |
| `kubectl rollout restart` of the API | No leaderless gap observed, no interleaving, no duplicate minutes. The scheduler never led. |
| API `/health/live` during the new leader's startup burst (leader vs follower) | p50 1.4 vs 1.4 ms, p99 6 vs 5 ms. One stall of about 300 ms on the leader (follower max 20 ms). |

About that stall: it is a one-time cost when a process first becomes leader, while the callbacks' lazy imports (about 1,100 modules) load. A second round in the same process imported nothing. In steady state the only recurring stall is the hourly bundle-preview cleanup building an S3 client (about 75 ms), the same cost any S3-touching request already pays.

**Docker test stack:**
- **API-hosted control:** 95/95 scheduler-related e2e tests pass:
  - scheduler diagnostics and fixture workloads;
  - workflow scheduling, events;
  - SDK update, publish, summary backfill, Solution deploy.
  - The API container holds the lease. Platform jobs still ran on the scheduler, whose logs show it never started control.
- **Default mode:** the same core set passes.
- **Mixed hosts:** a scheduler hosting control next to an API hosting control. The scheduler led, was SIGKILLed, and the API took over after 34.8 s with no interleaved or duplicate runs.

**Tests:**
- `tests/unit/scheduler/` (29), against real Postgres:
  - two-replica crash failover, rolling handoff, total partition (the stale leader stops before the successor starts);
  - lease-deadline, catalog pinning, supervisor restart and shutdown.
- Failover and concurrent-reconcile tests: 5/5 repeated runs green.
- `test_cron_scheduler.py` (16): dedupe across leaders, catch-up after failover, the bounded window, DST, and occurrences fired by an older image.
- `test_kubernetes_reconcile_concurrency.py`: two reconcilers race over five queued builds against real row locks, giving exactly 2 Jobs, each created and started once.
- Also run:
  - manifest and renderer tests, `test_access_list.py`, scheduler diagnostics e2e;
  - migration, contract and schema tripwires.

**Commands:**
- `./test.sh pr-preflight`: backend unit 9,832 passed, client unit 3,959 passed, changed e2e passed. Its CodeQL step flagged 4 test-hygiene notes; I fixed them, and `scripts/codeql-local.sh --rebuild --changed-only --fail-on-alerts` now reports 0.

prs.title: Accept workflow and agent runs durably before dispatch (#769 stage 2a-2b)
prs.body:
## Product Updates

- [ ] Highlight
- [ ] Other
- [x] Omit — reliability infrastructure. A queued run is no longer lost if a message or Redis entry is lost. Runs also appear as Pending from the moment they are accepted, rather than only once a worker starts them.

## Summary

Stage 2, slices 2a (workflow runs) and 2b (agent runs) of #769 (plan: `docs/plans/2026-10-22-769-stage2-durable-dispatch.md`). **Stacked on #1031**: its base is `769-api-control-stage1`, and it will be retargeted to `main` once #1031 merges.

Before this change, immediate workflow runs were Redis-first: only a 1-hour Redis blob and a RabbitMQ message existed until a worker started the run. A lost message, an expired or flushed blob, or an API crash between the two made the run vanish without trace.

**Acceptance**
- Every immediate workflow or inline-code run is now accepted as a `PENDING` Execution plus a `work_dispatches` row holding its execution context, committed together. Callers include HTTP execute, SDK nested runs, endpoints, forms, data providers, event deliveries and integration test runs.
- The API then publishes on the fast path, and the direct API → RabbitMQ → warm-worker path stays.
- A failed publish no longer fails an accepted request.

**Claim**
- The worker claims in one transaction: the run moves `PENDING → RUNNING` and the dispatch is deleted, returning its payload.
- A duplicate or stale delivery, or a run cancelled while pending, finds nothing to claim.
- If a sync caller's run ended before any worker started it, the caller is woken.

**Reconciler** (in stage 1's control plane, on every control replica)
- Settles candidates one at a time in short transactions, locking the run before its dispatch (the claim's order). It publishes after commit, so no lock is held across the broker.
- A lost hand-off is republished after 60 s.
- A message lost by the broker is republished after 30 minutes, at most 3 deliveries. After that the run fails visibly, with live update, queue removal and sync wake-up, instead of vanishing as it used to after Redis's 1-hour TTL.
- Started work is never replayed.

**Deferred promoter**
- Stages dispatches in its `PENDING` transaction. This fixes the existing hole where a crash after the promoter's commit stranded rows forever (`started_at` NULL never matched the sweep).

**Agent runs (2b)**
- An agent run's context now lives in a `work_dispatches` row committed with its `queued` AgentRun, instead of only in Redis.
- The worker takes the context by deleting the dispatch inside its existing locked claim transaction.
- A Redis or RabbitMQ outage no longer fails an accepted agent run. Previously the run was marked failed. Now the reconciler publishes it, or fails it visibly after its delivery budget and wakes a sync caller.

**Connections**
- Acceptance uses a small dedicated pool (`BIFROST_DATABASE_DISPATCH_POOL_SIZE`, default 4 + 6). Request handlers that still hold a main-pool connection never wait on each other for a second one.

**One-release mixed-version bridge** (to be removed in stage 5)
- The API still writes the Redis pending record (best-effort) before publishing, so an older worker runs the durable row through its existing `execution_record_exists` claim.
- New workers still accept legacy Redis-first messages.

## Evidence

**Failure drills on the live Docker stack:**
- RabbitMQ stopped during acceptance: the request was accepted with a `PENDING` row and pending dispatch. It completed 61 s after the broker restarted, when the reconciler published it.
- Redis `FLUSHALL` after acceptance with the worker stopped: the run completed (result `42`) with its context from PostgreSQL. Before this change it would have vanished.

- Agent run accepted with RabbitMQ stopped: the run stayed `queued` with a pending dispatch. About 66 s after the broker restarted, the reconciler published it and a worker claimed it, deleting the dispatch. The run then ended for its own reason (the drill passed no acting user).

**Mixed versions:** a worker running the pre-dispatch code and a new worker consumed the same new API concurrently. 55/55 execution e2e tests passed. The old worker ran 21 runs, and the reconciler then cleared their 21 leftover dispatches.

**Tests:**
- Agent and chat e2e, 216 passed:
  - agent enqueue, run-as, delegation lifecycle, children, visibility, pagination, management;
  - agent workflow tools, events, builtin events, chat, agents;
  - capability composition, usage summary, model failover;
  - `tests/e2e/scenarios`.
- `test_agent_run_dispatch.py` (3, real PostgreSQL) and the rewritten `test_agent_run_service.py` (13).
- Execution e2e, 224/224: executions, endpoints, data providers, forms, scheduled and deferred, scheduling flow, events, cancel, SDK reads, run identity, scope, embed, agent tool calls, integrations.
- `test_workflow_dispatch.py` (12), against real PostgreSQL:
  - commit before publish; broker failure, then reconciler publish; Redis outage;
  - claim-once and duplicate delivery; cancel before claim;
  - republish, then visible failure with notifications; dispatch left by an older worker;
  - the reconciler skipping a run that is being claimed (lock order); failed republish returning to pending;
  - cancelled sync run wake-up, with no wake-up for duplicates of started runs; org-scoped workflow filing.
- Promoter tests updated: a publish failure now leaves a durable dispatch instead of reverting.
- `./test.sh quality api` clean. Broader unit suites pass, including `test_access_list.py` with the flag-carrier registry updated.

**Latency (measured, the trade-off to review):**
- Acceptance alone: old Redis-first 0.5 ms against durable 4.3–5.5 ms p50. That is the commit.
- End-to-end trivial sync run (API → worker → result), 150 runs each: p50 about 39 → 43–46 ms, p95 about 47–55 → 57–62 ms. That is the API commit plus the worker's claim transaction replacing a Redis read.

An independent review's findings (pool pressure, duplicate publishes, lock-order deadlock, backlog amplification, unreported pre-start endings, org filing, redundant writes) are addressed in `36246686f`.

**Not run:** full backend e2e and browser suites (the merge queue will). Live Kind exercise of this slice comes with slice 2b.

prs.title: Reusable pool executors with on-demand Kubernetes workers (#769 stage 3a)
prs.body:
## Product Updates

- [ ] Highlight
- [ ] Other
- [x] Omit — opt-in runtime infrastructure (`BIFROST_EXECUTION_PLACEMENT=pool`). Default installations are unchanged. The only visible addition is one more scheduled maintenance task listed in Diagnostics.

## Summary

Stage 3a of #769 (plan: `docs/plans/2026-10-22-769-stage3-reusable-workers.md`). **Stacked on #1032**, which is stacked on #1031. Draft until stage 3b's failure drills land.

**Opt-in pool placement.** With `BIFROST_EXECUTION_PLACEMENT=pool`, accepted workflow and agent runs stay in PostgreSQL and are claimed by pool executors instead of being published to RabbitMQ. Placement is fixed per dispatch, so changing the setting never strands in-flight work.

**One executor, two forms** (`src/worker/pool_main.py`): the existing worker runtime, with a fresh process-pool child per run, the same SDK boundary and the same credentials.
- *Job*:
  - a controller-created `batch/v1` Job;
  - created suspended, its UID persisted, then started;
  - the pod admits itself once;
  - it drains itself to zero after the idle timeout, never mid-run.
- *Static* (`BIFROST_WORKER_FORM=static`): a long-running container that registers itself, for Docker installs and warm capacity. With this, the scheduler and worker containers can converge on one identical executor in stage 5.

**Claims**
- The claim uses `SKIP LOCKED` and requires the executor to be `ready`, so a draining executor can never claim.
- It honours the handler version and the broker worker's two existing limits: process-pool forks for workflow runs, `max_concurrency` for agent runs.
- A Redis wake hint removes the poll delay; it is never authority.

**Capacity controller** (control plane, every API replica)
- Launches Job workers for unclaimed demand within `BIFROST_POOL_MAX_WORKERS`, serialized by an advisory lock, and keeps `BIFROST_POOL_MIN_WORKERS` warm.
- Marks a worker that misses its start deadline or heartbeat, or whose Job vanished, as lost, then deletes its Job.
- The dispatch reconciler releases work a dead executor held. It fails runs no capacity picked up within 30 minutes, visibly.

**No dead resources**
- Finished worker Jobs have a TTL.
- An hourly task prunes ended executors and ends silent static ones.
- Dispatch rows exist only while unclaimed.

## Evidence

**Kind** (two API replicas hosting control, **no broker worker pods**, ceiling 3 × 2 slots, idle 45 s; `./test.sh kubernetes pool-experiment`):

| Phase | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Zero | 0 worker pods, 0 live executors |
| First run | worker launched from zero; cold start 12.6 s |
| Reuse | 3 more runs on the same pod in 3.5 s |
| Burst | 16 × 6 s runs in 27.4 s; peak 3 workers / 3 pods (the ceiling) |
| Idle | every worker drained itself (`retired`/`idle`); zero in 49 s |
| Drain race | a run accepted while its worker was draining finished on a fresh worker in 12.9 s; zero again in 47 s |

**Docker:** pool placement with one static executor and the broker worker stopped. 236 execution, agent, chat, event and scenario e2e tests passed (2 skipped).

**Latency** (end-to-end trivial sync run, 200 runs each, same stack):

| Path | p50 | p95 | p99 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Broker | 47 ms | 64–68 ms | 81–100 ms |
| Pool (static executor) | 55–57 ms | 86–94 ms | 109–128 ms |

Both paths are subsecond. Folding the pool's assignment and claim into one transaction is the next optimization. A cold Job worker takes about 12 s, so interactive runs need warm capacity: a static executor or `BIFROST_POOL_MIN_WORKERS`.

**Bugs found and fixed while driving it:**
- Executors used the wrong concurrency limit, which serialized short runs.
- Package-install broadcasts did not reach executors.
- The executor process was missing the placement setting, which stranded nested agent-tool runs.
- A wake hint could be lost, causing a 1 s stall.

**Tests:**
- `tests/unit/services/worker_pool/test_worker_pool.py` (13, real PostgreSQL plus a fake cluster):
  - placement never publishes; admission happens once;
  - each dispatch is claimed once across executors; draining executors never claim;
  - an unsupported handler version waits for a compatible executor;
  - static registration and claiming;
  - bounded launches under concurrent controllers, with the Job bound before it starts;
  - a silent worker is lost, its work released and its Job deleted;
  - the capacity deadline fails a run visibly;
  - pruning; the warm minimum.
- Kind renderer and manifest tests.
- Broader suites, 330 + 82: scheduler, execution, jobs, the access-list inventory, migration tripwires.
- `./test.sh quality api` clean.

**Remaining (3b):** cancellation, OOM, node loss, controller-restart and unschedulable-capacity drills, plus image-pull and idle-tail measurements.

## Summary

`shared/schema_gate.py` is meant to treat a database revision that this image does not know as "ahead", because a newer image migrated the database. Alembic reports an unknown revision with `ResolutionError`, which is a `RevisionError` and not a `CommandError`. The gate only caught `CommandError`, so it raised.

**Effect:** any older-image worker or scheduler that starts or restarts after a newer migration crash-loops. This breaks:
- rolling deploys, when an old pod restarts mid-rollout;

Found during the #769 stage 2 mixed-version check: a #1031-code worker would not start against a database migrated by #1032.

prs.title: Apply package changes from a desired generation in PostgreSQL (#769 stage 4a)
prs.body:
## Summary

Stage 4a of #769, stacked on #1033. Package installs reached workers only through a RabbitMQ fanout to exclusive, auto-delete queues. An executor that was not consuming at that moment missed the change for good, unless it restarted.

- **`package_changes`:** each install or uninstall is a row, and its id is the package generation.
  - The row is recorded in the request's transaction, together with the `requirements.txt` write.
  - Recording takes a transaction-scoped advisory lock, so generations commit in order and an executor never skips a lower id.
- **Executors** (`src/worker/pool_main.py`):
  - read the current generation *before* the pool installs requirements at boot, so a change committed in between is applied again (idempotent), never missed;
  - apply every newer change in order from a dedicated loop. It is separate from the heartbeat, because pip can run for minutes.
  - They reuse `PackageInstallConsumer.process_message`, so phase reporting and the UI progress are unchanged.
  - They report their generation on `execution_workers.package_generation`, and no longer consume the broadcast.
- **Broker workers** still take the broadcast, with the same `run_id`, until stage 5 retires RabbitMQ. Default installs see no change.

## Verification

- **Unit tests:**
  - changes are read in order;
  - a change is invisible until its transaction commits;
  - concurrent changes commit in generation order. That test fails with the lock removed.
  - The executor loop applies only newer changes, in order, and retries the same change after an unexpected error.
  - The router records a change that shares the broadcast's `run_id`, for both install and uninstall.
  - Result: 37 passed across the package, router, consumer and worker-pool suites.
- **Live, Docker pool mode with three static executors:**
  1. Froze executor B (`docker pause`) and installed `humanize==4.13.0` through `POST /api/packages/install`.
  2. Executor A applied it, reaching generation 1, while B was still frozen.
  3. Started a new executor C, then unfroze B. All three reached generation 1, and B caught up from its loop without restarting.
  4. 30 concurrent runs importing `humanize` all succeeded, 10 on each executor.
  5. Uninstalled with B frozen again. All three reached generation 2, the package was gone everywhere, and runs failed with `No module named 'humanize'`.
- **Broker path unchanged:** package e2e passed 5/5 (`test_package_available_after_installation`, nested module update, requirements helper, package list).
- **Runtime checklist:** passed in pool mode on this branch.
- ruff and pyright are clean on the changed files; migration tripwires pass.

prs.title: Make agent-run summaries a durable dispatch family (#769 stage 4b)
prs.body:
## Summary

Stage 4b of #769, stacked on #1035.

**Problem.** A summary was a fire-and-forget RabbitMQ message, published after the run committed.
- If that publish failed, or the message was lost, the summary stayed `pending` forever. Nothing swept for them.
- In pool placement (#1033), executors never consumed the summary queue. A pool-only install would therefore strand every summary.
- There was no claim, so a duplicate delivery summarized the run twice and wrote two AIUsage rows.

**Staging.** Summaries are now the `agent_summary` dispatch family (`src/services/execution/summary_dispatch.py`).
- The dispatch is staged in the transaction that completes the run (agent runs and delegated runs), regenerates it, or backfills it.
- The insert is `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`. A second request for the same run is a no-op and can never fail the run's completion commit.

**Claim.** Under the run's lock, the claim moves the summary from `pending` to `generating` and takes the dispatch. A duplicate delivery, or a run that moved on, skips.

**Reconciler.** It republishes lost broker hand-offs and fails summaries that nothing picked up. A backfill summary nobody picked up counts as failed against its backfill.

**Pool executors:**
- They claim live summaries and backfill summaries through separate handlers, one slot each. This matches the broker consumers' prefetch of 1, and a large backfill never delays live summaries.
- A lost executor's in-flight summary is requested again, because a summary has no effect outside its run. It keeps its backfill membership.

**Backfill membership** moves onto the run as `agent_runs.summary_backfill_job_id`, with a partial index. Outcomes are counted however a summary is delivered or recovered.

**Bug fixed: backfill counters lost updates.** `record_backfill_outcome` did an unlocked read-modify-write on the counters. Found live: with two executors, 4 summaries completed but the job stuck at 3/4, so its PlatformJob waited forever. Two executors is the Docker default from stage 5, so it now locks the job row.

**Dead code removed.** The `agent-tuning-chat` consumer never had a publisher. Removed: the consumer, its queue name, `enqueue_tune_chat`, and the KEDA trigger. The runbook documents deleting the empty queue, and the stage-5 cleanup list includes it.

**Compatibility.** Broker workers keep consuming both queues. Until stage 5 they also accept messages without a dispatch id from an older API.

## Verification

- **Unit tests,** new in `test_summary_dispatch.py`, `test_backfill_tracker.py` and `test_pool_main_summaries.py`:
  - claim once, and a duplicate skips;
  - a second request is a no-op;
  - a run that moved on is not claimed, and its dispatch is taken away;
  - reconciler waiting semantics;
  - backfill stages dispatches before handing them off;
  - the handler counts outcomes against the run's backfill;
  - a lost executor's summary is re-requested on the backfill handler;
  - an unclaimed backfill summary counts as failed;
  - concurrent outcomes are all counted. This test failed with 2/2 of 8 before the lock.
  - Executor capacity: a running backfill summary never blocks a live one.
- **Affected unit suites:** 871 passed.
- **E2E:** backfill, regenerate, agent-management, delegation-lifecycle and capability-composition suites, 29 passed. The backfill e2e caught a missing flush, which is fixed.
- **Live, Docker pool mode.** Two static executors ran with the broker worker stopped, against an OpenAI-compatible stub model.
  - 4 agent runs completed, and all 4 summaries reached `completed`. Each run has exactly one summarizer usage row, and no dispatches remain.
  - 3 backfill rounds each completed 4/4, with the PlatformJob `succeeded`.
  - The runtime checklist passed.
- ruff and pyright are clean on all changed files. `alembic check` shows no drift on the changed tables.

**Not yet run:** the Kind (Job worker) pass. It will run with the other stage-4 families before this leaves draft.

## Summary

Stage 4c of #769, stacked on #1036. The executor (`src/worker/pool_main.py`) now also runs what only the scheduler and the broker worker hosted:

prs.title: Accept an event delivery's run in the delivery's transaction (#769 stage 4d)
prs.body:
## Summary

Stage 4d of #769, stacked on #1037.

**Problem.** Every event caller committed the event and its deliveries, accepted each run in a separate transaction, then committed `QUEUED` and the run id later. That caused three problems:
- **Lost run records.** A crash in between left a workflow run with no delivery record of it. The delivery stayed `PENDING` with no `execution_id`, was swept to `FAILED`, and a manual retry ran the workflow a second time.
- **Cron.** `QUEUED` stayed uncommitted across later sources. One failing source lost earlier sources' run ids while their runs went ahead.
- **Retry and manual delivery** re-queued every pending sibling on the event, including deliveries another caller was still queueing.

**Fix.**
- **Acceptance split.** Workflow and agent-run acceptance now stage rows into the caller's session (`stage_system_workflow_execution`, `stage_agent_run_request`) and hand off after commit. `enqueue_agent_run` keeps its contract by doing both in its own transaction. `enqueue_system_workflow_execution` had only this caller and is replaced.
- **`queue_event_deliveries`:**
  - stages each delivery's run in a savepoint, together with its `QUEUED` status and run id;
  - returns a `QueuedDeliveries` batch whose hand-offs and broadcast run after the caller commits;
  - accepts `delivery_ids` to limit queueing to given deliveries.
- **Callers.** The hook route, `emit_event`, cron (one commit per source), retry and manual `create_delivery` each commit once, then hand off. Retry and manual delivery queue only their own delivery. Retry also clears a stale `agent_run_id`.
- **Unchanged.** If queueing fails outright, the event is still recorded with pending deliveries. The webhook still returns 202, and `emit_event` and cron still report the error.
- **Access inventory.** Updated for the moved hand-offs: `_pending_run`, `_context_fields` and `stage_agent_run_request` replace `_publish_pending`, `enqueue_workflow_execution` and `enqueue_agent_run`. Each keeps its disposition.

## Verification

- **Unit tests against the real database** (`test_delivery_acceptance.py`):
  - a crash (rollback) before the commit leaves no execution and no dispatch, and the delivery stays `PENDING` with no run id;
  - the commit makes the run, its dispatch and the delivery's `QUEUED` and run id visible together;
  - a delivery that cannot be queued fails alone while the others commit;
  - a retry never queues a pending sibling.
- Old-contract tests were rewritten to assert the new order (queue, commit, hand off) for the hook route, `emit_event` and cron, plus the retry and processor fakes.
- **Results:**
  - unit: 493 passed across every suite touching events, cron, acceptance and the access inventory;
  - e2e: 66 passed across the events, event retry, subscription filters, SDK and CLI events, scheduling flow and scheduler fixture suites;
  - e2e scenarios: 55 passed.
- ruff and pyright are clean on the changed files.

**Not yet run:** the Kind (Job worker) pass. It will run with the other stage-4 families before this leaves draft.

- Every dispatch is pool-placed.

- Each entry point keeps its own health files: the worker's readiness file, and the scheduler's liveness heartbeat and readiness file. Existing healthchecks and probes therefore pass. Without this, the scheduler's liveness probe would kill it.

**The Kubernetes loops follow the permission, not a flag.** The on-demand worker controller and the build-Job controller start in every process whose service account may manage Jobs. This is checked with a `SelfSubjectAccessReview`.

- the API pod's own namespace and image;

Both containers start as executors and their v1.4.1 healthchecks pass.

## Product Updates

- [ ] Highlight
- [x] Other — Bifrost no longer uses RabbitMQ: executors claim all work from PostgreSQL. Existing installs keep working with their old compose file or manifests; the leftover broker can be removed (see the runbook).

## Summary

Stage 5b of #769: retire RabbitMQ. Since 5a (#1039) nothing consumes the broker, so this removes the code, topology and one-release bridges, and fixes two gaps the claim model had left. Design: `docs/plans/2026-10-22-769-stages4-5-convergence.md` (Stage 5b design).

**Removed**
- `src.jobs.rabbitmq`, the consumer base classes, the package-install broadcast, the RabbitMQ readiness check, `rabbitmq_url`, and the `aio-pika` dependency (no production workspace imports it).
- The Redis bridges: the pending-execution record and agent-run context written for older workers, the Redis-only "pending receipt" read and cancel paths, and the consumer's Redis-first message path. Every run has its row and dispatch from acceptance (stage 2). The cancel endpoint's response is now always a `WorkflowExecution`.
- RabbitMQ from every compose file, the Kubernetes manifests, KEDA and the Kind harness built on it, the test stack, and the docs. The Kind build-Jobs overlay drops its now-unused controller account (the API runs that controller).

**Existing installs keep working.** Settings ignore a leftover `BIFROST_RABBITMQ_URL`, and the execution template still scrubs it from children because it carries credentials. A leftover `rabbitmq` service or Deployment is unused. The runbook and README say how to remove the broker, its volume and KEDA, and that dead-lettered messages are not replayed.

**Dispatch table.** `queue`, `status`, `publish_count` and `last_published_at` are no longer written. 5a pods still write them during a rolling upgrade, so this release relaxes them; the next release drops them (and the `execution_record_exists` message field).

**Memory gating restored.** Under RabbitMQ a fork refused for memory pressure was NACKed to another worker; with PostgreSQL claims it left the run RUNNING with no child.
- An executor over `memory_pressure_threshold` claims nothing new and reports it in its heartbeat (`execution_workers.memory_pressured`).
- The worker controller does not count a pressured executor's free slots, so it starts a worker Job for the work left waiting.
- A fork refused after a claim hands the run back: RUNNING → PENDING, a fresh dispatch, the claim record removed.

**Executor drain** ends with the process pool's drain, so in-flight results are recorded and runs still active at the grace deadline are recorded as interrupted, as the broker consumer did.

**Rollback.** Init now skips migrations when the database is newer than its image (the same rule as the #1034 schema gate). Rolling back to a release before this one across a migration needs a downgrade with the newer image first; the runbook has the commands.

**Also fixed:**
- A cron scheduler test that failed when a run crossed a minute boundary (earlier tests left every-minute schedules enabled).
- Unit-only runs now stop the API as well as the executors. Since 5a the API's control plane reconciles dispatches; CI caught it re-placing a unit test's dispatch before the test did. The next state reset starts it again.
- The Kind pool experiment and drills assumed stage 3 (no static executors, ceiling 3, scale to zero); they now prove the unified setup (below).

- `./test.sh unit`: 9843 passed. `./test.sh quality api`: pyright 0 errors, ruff clean. Client `tsc` and `lint` clean; types regenerated from this branch's API. Operation inventory and skill appendices unchanged.
- **Docker upgrade rehearsal:** v1.4.1 with its own compose file (RabbitMQ still in it) and seeded data → this image only. The seeded workflow runs; full runtime checklist green; warm latency matches 5a measured side by side.
- **Docker rollback** to 5a (downgrade with this image, then 5a): seeded workflow and checklist green.
- **Kind upgrade** from 5a with its KEDA and RabbitMQ still deployed, including a 5a worker Job still running (mixed versions): checklist green; then the runbook's removal of KEDA and the broker, checklist green again.
- **Kind rollback** to 5a: seeded workflow and checklist green.
- **Stage 5c proof, Kind with the base manifests' defaults** (`pool-experiment`): two static executors (20 slots) plus the warm minimum of 1 worker Job; a burst of 40 runs × 30 s scaled worker Jobs to exactly 6 (never more) and finished in 60 s; a run accepted while the extra Jobs drained completed in 0.1 s; the pool returned to 1.

prs.title: Recover work an earlier release left in RabbitMQ (#769)
prs.body:
## Product Updates

- [ ] Highlight
- [x] Other — Upgrading from an earlier release no longer loses runs it left queued: the API moves them out of RabbitMQ once at start, and runs scheduled ahead keep running. Keep RabbitMQ until the API logs that it drained.
- [ ] Omit

## Summary

Part of #769. Releases before the unified runtime (v1.4.1 and earlier) queued workflow runs, agent runs and summaries in RabbitMQ. After #1040, nothing read them, so an install upgraded with work waiting lost it.

**Drain.** When `BIFROST_RABBITMQ_URL` is set, each API replica runs `drain_legacy_broker` once from its lifespan. It waits for the schema, tries the broker 3 times, drains every old queue until it's empty, disconnects and stops. It doesn't poll again. Each message becomes the durable dispatch the current release would have accepted, then is acknowledged. A message it can't recover stays queued, and the next start tries again. Several replicas draining at once is safe: each message goes to one consumer, and a subject has at most one dispatch.

**Lineage.** Earlier releases recorded only the user a run executes as. The runtime refuses runs without lineage (#996), so in the first rehearsal every recovered run, and every run v1.4.1 had scheduled ahead, failed with an engine-token 401. The new rule is `shared.run_lineage.recorded_user_lineage`:

- A recorded person becomes the run user and starter.
- The system account runs as a schedule does: the workflow's identity, else the organization's default.
- Agent runs use their caller, else the organization's default identity.
- The run is its own root.

The drain applies this rule to messages. Migration `20261023_legacy_run_lineage` backfills waiting `Scheduled`/`Pending` rows.

**Cancelled runs.** A run cancelled while queued is recorded as Cancelled, as v1.4.1 did.

`README.md` and `docs/runbooks/kubernetes-worker-deployment.md` now say to keep the broker until it has drained. During a Kubernetes rolling upgrade, an older API pod can still queue work after the new pods drain. The runbook says to check the queues after the rollout and restart the API if any still hold messages.

prs.title: Executors admit work by memory (#769 stage 6)
prs.body:
## Product Updates

- [ ] Highlight
- [x] Other — Executors now take work by memory instead of fixed counts. Each workflow learns how much memory its runs use, and its settings can set it. A run that would exhaust an executor is stopped or given a worker with room, work no executor can hold fails at once, and Diagnostics shows runs waiting for capacity.
- [ ] Omit

## Summary

Part of #769, stage 6 (spec: `docs/plans/2026-10-23-769-stage6-resource-requests.md`). Every container already runs the same executor; this makes all of them admit work by memory, with one budget per executor and no count caps.

**The gate** (`src/worker/admission.py`). Every kind of work goes through it: workflow runs, agent runs, summaries, local platform jobs and services.

1. Work reserves memory. A workflow run reserves its typical peak growth (learned per workflow, 1/10 decay, reset on code change; 64 MiB if never measured; the workflow's `memory_request_mib` setting overrides). If it is actually using more, it reserves that instead, sampled every 250 ms.
2. An executor claims work only if the reservation fits its free budget and its real memory is under 85%. Its free budget is 85% of the container, minus itself, minus what its work reserves.
3. Once an executor holds two pieces of work, it waits for the last run to reach its child, plus 100 ms, before claiming again (Temporal's `rampThrottle`).
4. At 95% real memory, the executor stops the run or service that grew most.
5. A run killed for memory learns the executor's budget less the 16 MiB margin, so its next run fits an executor alone. "Killed for memory" means stopped by rule 4, killed by the kernel, or lost with a Job worker Kubernetes reports OOMKilled. Any other loss teaches nothing.

Claims are serialized: a loop reads the free budget, claims and holds before any other loop can claim. A service is held before its child forks.

**Lost executors.**
- An executor is lost after 30 s without a heartbeat, but only once the control loop judging it has itself reached the database for 30 s without a break. A database outage therefore never marks every executor lost.
- Heartbeats use the database clock.
- The dispatch reconciler now ends static executors at that rule. This replaces the hourly 10-minute sweep and the separate 2-minute silence rule.
- A result is written only while the run is still running and the writing executor still holds its claim, so a lost executor's late result never overwrites the loss.
- An executor told it is lost stops its runs instead of draining them.

**Sizing and visibility.**
- A Job launched for a dispatch takes it whatever budget it measured, and the Job baseline learns from every Job.
- A sized Job always drains when idle and is never the warm minimum.
- Work no executor can hold fails within seconds: runs at any age, queued local platform jobs, and services. A too-large service is blocked `too_large` until an executor can hold it. A draining executor's budget is not capacity.
- Platform jobs waiting for memory count as launch demand.
- A run waiting for capacity is no longer failed as "stuck" at 10 minutes; its 30-minute claim deadline decides.
- Diagnostics shows runs waiting and the oldest wait, and recommends capacity after a minute.

An independent review (Fable) of the first cut found the accounting sound. It found one blocker, that killed runs taught nothing, and five majors; all are fixed here. The runbook now covers Kubernetes' whole-container OOM (`memory.oom.group`), `singleProcessOOMKill` (1.32+), and Docker executors budgeting from the host.

Removed settings (`max_workers`, `max_concurrency`, `pool_worker_slots`, the platform-job slots and admission ratio, `max_service_workers`) are ignored if still set. The migration is expand-only.

### Verification

- **Kind pressure test** (`./test.sh kubernetes pressure-test`, report kept at `/tmp/769-pressure-3-report.json`):
  - Warm-floor sync p50 48 ms, p99 86 ms.
  - Learning: 8/8 runs; light 21 MiB, heavy 307 MiB.
  - A sized Job ran a 1,731 MiB request.
  - Too-large work failed within seconds.
  - Understated burst (12 runs using 200 MiB against a 32 MiB request): 12/12, no out-of-memory kill. It learned 208 MiB, and the repeat burst went 12/12.
  - 8-minute mixed ramp with an API pod and a busy worker pod killed: 919/920. The only failure was the killed worker's run; peak 2 Jobs.
  - The first run of this test (before these fixes) whole-pod-OOMed the scheduler executor in the understated phase.
- **Docker kill drill:** SIGKILLed the worker container mid-run. Its 2 runs failed visibly 34 s later, the other executor's 2 runs succeeded, and the worker came back as a new incarnation. This drill is why only OOMKilled losses teach.
- **`./test.sh e2e`:** 2,365 passed, 2 errors (service owner-loss fixture still passing the removed `free_bytes`). Fixed; that file then passed 3/3.

prs.title: Harden stage 6 against production timing edges (#769)
prs.body:
## Product Updates

- [ ] Highlight
- [ ] Other
- [x] Omit — Hardens #1044 against production-only timing edges before any release carried it.

## Summary

Part of #769. This addresses a second independent review (Fable) of stage 6's final implementation (#1044 plus hotfix #1045, both live in production). The review looked for the same kind of bug as the rollout one: a healthy executor declared lost, or work failed, by timing that only appears in production. A final review of this PR then found one more edge, also fixed here.

**Majors**
- **Heartbeats use their own database connection.** They now run on a separate single-connection engine. Before, they waited in the run pool, whose 30 s checkout timeout equals the lost rule, so a busy, healthy executor could be declared lost. Each heartbeat call is bounded, so a connection hung on a dead network does not stop the next one.
- **A database error while claiming no longer ends the executor and its runs.** The claim loop backs off like the other loops. One case needs care: a claim can commit while the executor never hears back. To handle it, the executor remembers what it started over the last 10 minutes. After a failed claim, it fails visibly a workflow run it claimed but never started (that run's dispatch went with the claim), and hands an agent run or summary back to the queue.
- **Reachability is measured by reaching the database each pass** (`SELECT 1`). A slow Kubernetes API or Redis no longer keeps lost detection off. One worker's reconcile failure no longer stops the others.
- **Work is too large only if no executor live within the last 10 minutes could hold it.** A big executor that is restarting or draining no longer fails its work.

**Minors**
- `pip list` runs off the event loop.
- A sync caller of a run ended with a lost executor hears at once instead of waiting out its timeout.
- Claim rows are indexed by `(worker_id, subject_id)` for the result-write check (migration `20261024_claims_by_subject`).
- A lost executor cancels its agent work.

**Test fix**
- The embedding model-listing tests no longer need live DNS. One failed in a full run on a host with flaky DNS.

The handoff doc records that stage 6 is live, plus one deferred finding: static executors register `ready` before they can claim.

### Verification

- `./test.sh pr-preflight`: green (unit 9,907; quality clean; CodeQL 0 for Python and TypeScript).
- `./test.sh e2e` on the branch before the last commit: 2,367 passed. The last commit touches only the claim loop's error path and the heartbeat call; its unit tests cover both.
- New tests:
  - a claim whose reply was lost is released, and started work is left alone;
  - a claim error does not end the executor;
  - a hung heartbeat does not stop the next one;
  - reachability is measured by database access;
  - one worker's failure does not stop the others;
  - an executor restarting or draining still counts as capacity;
  - a sync caller of a lost run hears at once;
  - a lost executor cancels its agent work.

Part of #769. During the production rollout of #1048, a cold scheduler executor heartbeated normally until its process template was ready (03:26:10). prs.title: Replace worker Jobs running an older build after an upgrade (#1052)
prs.body:
## Product Updates

- [ ] Highlight
- [x] Other — After an upgrade on Kubernetes, worker Jobs running the previous build are replaced automatically once their replacement is ready, and their runs finish first; drains no longer cut off runs longer than five minutes.
- [ ] Omit

## Summary

Closes #1052. Design (reviewed twice by Fable): `docs/plans/2026-10-24-1052-replace-outdated-worker-jobs.md`.

**Replace worker Jobs running an older build.**
- **What counts as outdated:** an admitted Job is outdated when no live controller runs its build and the controller that launched it is gone.
  - A worker reports its build (`BIFROST_VERSION`) when it is admitted.
  - The controller that creates a Job is recorded with the Job's UID.
  - Controllers publish themselves as live in Redis, on Redis's clock.
  - So a same-build restart replaces nothing, a rolling upgrade replaces Jobs only after the last old replica stops, and rollback is symmetric.
  - A Job launched by a live controller is never replaced, so replacement cannot loop.
- **Replacement order:** the warm minimum launches current Jobs first. Outdated Jobs drain as `rotated` once a replacement has started its pool and can claim. Jobs are never deleted.
- **`:latest` installs:** worker Jobs copy the controller container's `imagePullPolicy`, so they pull the moved tag.

**Drains let runs finish.** A drain the platform asks for (idle, rotated, maximum lifetime) waits for runs with no deadline of its own. The 300 s grace now starts only at SIGTERM, including when SIGTERM arrives mid-drain. The API warns once when a drain with active runs passes the maximum lifetime.

**Leftovers from #1052:**
- Static executors register `starting` and become `ready` once their pool is up and measured.
- The Kind build experiment's `--restart-controller` deletes the API pod that isn't running the workload.
- `WorkflowExecutionRequest.code` is now described as plain text (contract fingerprint refreshed; cosmetic).
- Dropping `slots` / `job_slots` is deferred to #1053, since v1.4.1 and the current images still read them during a rolling upgrade.

**Migration:** adds `execution_workers.version` and `launched_by` (both nullable).

**Rollout note:** controllers from earlier releases don't publish themselves, so on this first rollout the new controller rotates their Jobs during the rollout, not after it. The replaced Job runs the old code, so it still has the 300 s grace: check that no long run is on the warm Job before promoting.

## Verification

- **Unit tests:**
  - `./test.sh tests/unit/services/worker_pool/test_worker_pool.py tests/unit/test_pool_main_hosting.py`: 77 passed. New tests cover:
    - the outdated rule;
    - live publish, expiry and withdrawal;
    - launch-then-drain through a full `reconcile()`;
    - waiting until the replacement can claim;
    - a same-build restart;
    - no loop while the launcher is live;
    - a Job reserved for a dispatch;
    - a warm minimum of 0;
    - the current Job idle-draining first;
    - the adopted-Job launcher;
    - the pull policy;
    - static `starting` → `ready`;
    - the drain with no deadline, SIGTERM mid-drain, and lost mid-drain.
  - Neighboring and tripwire tests: scheduler control, Kubernetes control, the other pool_main tests, service claims, startup, alembic single head, migration tombstones, contract version, execution request contract, contracts parity, access list. All pass.
- **`./test.sh pr-preflight`:**
  - The full unit run (9,993 passed) and lint/types passed.
  - Its one failure was the unclassified Redis read in `test_access_list`, since fixed (74/74 pass).
  - `./test.sh quality api`: clean.
- **Kind (production image), `./test.sh kubernetes pool-drills --only upgrade`:**
  - **Same-tag upgrade** (the image tag moved to a new `BIFROST_VERSION` build, like a new `:latest`), with the warm Job running a 400 s workflow:
    - exactly one replacement was launched;
    - the old Job drained as `rotated` only after the replacement could claim;
    - a new run was served in 0.1 s;
    - the 400 s run succeeded past the old 300 s grace;
    - the old Job retired, with no `lost` rows.
  - **Rollback:** the same, symmetric.
  - Before the claim-readiness fix, the new run took 8.4 s. That confirmed the review finding.
- **Kind failure drills** (kill, controller_restart, oom, unschedulable): all pass.

## Product Updates

## Summary

Automatic chat and background runs now share Pydantic's native CodeMode and ToolSearch. Remove the private sandbox SDK, callable renderer, discovery protocol, and dispatcher. Native discovery adapts Bifrost's existing capability ranking; business execution keeps the existing authorization, workflow/MCP dispatch, cancellation, and audit paths.

The remaining adapter handles stored JSON tool definitions, bounded Python names, JSON-or-text nested values, and the model-result boundary. Full nested values are available to code; the outer model result retains its cap. Native child delegation stays outside business code. Public MCP search/execute formats and arbitrary workflow return values remain unchanged. Existing workers run the pinned Monty interpreter without Bubblewrap or a new service.

Align the declared Harness version with the already-locked AI 2.55 / Harness 0.55 / Monty 1.3 runtime. No runtime dependency upgrade.

## Evidence

The complete frozen DeepSeek Flash comparison contains 207 attempts: 23 synthetic cases × three arms × three repetitions, with no repeats or replacement attempts.

| Metric, 69 attempts per arm | Current Automatic | Native Automatic | Direct Tools |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Requested data and required receipts correct | 66 | 68 | 67 |
| Captured input tokens | 1,653,574 | 981,051 | 3,186,945 |
| Cost from captured usage | $0.068495274 | $0.040527084 | $0.151541778 |
| Unsupported prose findings | 3 | 0 | 0 |

Native captured cost is 40.8% lower than current and 73.3% lower than direct; captured input is 40.7% and 69.2% lower. Model-visible tool-return bytes are 91.0% lower than direct, with 85.7% less cumulative rereading. Independent final review resummed every captured provider response and checked the frozen inputs, artifacts, adjudication, and source integrity.

These are synthetic, workload-weighted results. Large reports drive most savings; several small workloads cost more than direct tools. Two provider timeouts, one in each CodeMode arm, remain counted failures with unknown billing; cost percentages describe captured usage, not a proven complete invoice. Strict JSON-only formatting remains weaker than direct tools: candidate 6/33 whole-message JSON outputs, current 0/33, direct 16/33; explicitly JSON-only MCP/workflow attempts are 2/6, 0/6, and 5/6. Fenced correct data are not claimed to satisfy JSON-only consumers.

prs.title: Reduce idle worker memory with API-controlled execution
prs.body:
## Product Updates

- [ ] Highlight
- [x] Other — Reduce idle worker memory while preserving workflow, service, agent, and platform-job execution.
- [ ] Omit

## Summary

Make the thin physical runner the default through the existing API, worker, scheduler, Compose, and Kubernetes entrypoints. Workers retain their full image and execute the same workflows, services, and registered job handlers; durable claims, SDK authorization, and execution control are hosted by the API instead of being imported into every idle worker. Heavy platform-job dependencies live in short-lived child processes.

Authenticate launcher enrollment and fence API owners with database-time leases. Reconcile live children and unacknowledged results after disconnects and API restarts, preserve cancellation and drain, and keep API-agent capacity separate from physical worker capacity. Keep existing Kubernetes Role placements working and enroll worker Jobs automatically. Legacy scheduler-role deployments load controller dependencies only in their dedicated helper, preserving the lean launcher import boundary.

## Validation

- 425 focused runtime unit tests passed; access-inventory/Kubernetes-manifest tripwires passed another 81 checks. Follow-up owner-lease coverage passed 42 focused tests. Python lint and types passed.
- Merge-queue failures led to a real lease-renewal repair: admission still pauses on three-second-old telemetry, while connected owner renewal uses its existing twenty-second window. The full failing shard prefix passed 637 live tests, then 97 SDK/retention/MCP/identity tests passed. SDK functional and authorization assertions remain intact with the default HTTP transport.
- A later queue run exposed a package-recycle/monitor race. Liveness now shares the replacement lock; genuine template crashes preserve automatic replacement and live child handles, while failed replacement exits for container recovery. The deterministic regression plus recovery/fencing checks passed 56 tests, and the package → SDK → identity/child-isolation live sequence passed 19 tests.
- Live coverage exercised all 23 registered PlatformJob handlers, workflows and SDK calls, service lifecycle, real agents and summaries, package install/removal on both physical templates, reconnect cancellation, and a 33 MiB result with a single persisted side effect. A final five-test build/Git/recovery/SDK recheck passed after correcting stale test-container state on reset.
- Isolated Kind: 53 workflows across three worker Jobs survived replacement of both API pods, retaining Job/Pod identities and exactly one claim each. Two real app deploys in isolated 2 GiB pods and an SDK update succeeded while replacing an API controller; maintenance work completed alongside builds.
- Current whole-container working set after the broad workload: about 85 MiB per physical executor and 562 MiB for the shared API. Final local warm workflow medians: 121 ms simple / 142 ms with an SDK config read. One cached-image worker startup: 7.25 s, excluding image pull/scheduling and backing-service startup.
- Conditions, limitations, exact focused commands, failure dispositions, image/source identities, and machine-readable evidence: [default-runner report](docs/benchmarks/2026-10-25-default-remote-runner.md).

Full local backend/client/browser suites were not run; the merge queue is the complete-suite gate. Provider fixtures verify integration behavior, not every provider option. No production deployment or hosted infrastructure is included.

prs.title: Preserve thin-runner results through serialization and owner loss
prs.body:
## Product Updates

- [x] Other — Workflow results containing dates, UUIDs, and decimals complete correctly on thin workers, including after controller ownership loss.

## Summary

SDK responses can contain Python datetimes nested inside workflow results. The new remote runner used plain JSON serialization before transport, so an otherwise successful workflow could lose its terminal result and repeatedly fail to replay it after reconnecting. A safe production organizations-read benchmark exposed this; production was rolled back and scheduled promotion paused.

Use the existing execution-result contract (`json.dumps(..., default=str)`) for control envelopes and fragmented messages. Preserve the existing JSONB string representation without importing application dependencies into the launcher. Strengthen the existing live organizations test to return its SDK datetime through the real child/launcher/API boundary.

On telemetry loss, an API owner could also retire the physical worker while its launcher retained results for replay. Detach that lost owner without retiring the durable worker row. Ordinary drained retirement remains intact. Strengthen the existing 33 MiB result test to wait for actual owner loss/release with a still-valid lease before reconnecting; require one execution, one side effect, and successful replay.

## Validation

All commands ran through the Docker test stack using its existing dependency image and current source mounts:

- Three serialization regression cases failed before the JSON fix. The ownership-loss test failed before the retirement guard (14 adjacent cases passed).

## Product Updates

- [x] Other — Workflows continue through queue-display outages, and event delivery status follows the actual workflow or agent run.

## Summary

A production Redis DNS timeout while publishing UI queue positions aborted a claimed workflow before its child started. Its durable execution remained Running while the healthy worker had no child or active run. Treat UI queue-removal failure as a logged notification failure and continue the already-owned execution; PostgreSQL remains authoritative.

The same investigation found event cleanup marking any delivery older than five minutes Failed, including long-running workflows and agents. Exclude canonical live owners, reconcile missed terminal callbacks through the existing workflow completion path, and fail only abandoned deliveries without an owner. Share row-locked completion bookkeeping with normal workflow/agent callbacks: fence the current run, avoid counting a late callback twice, and clear stale errors when the canonical outcome repairs an old false failure. Workflow failure built-in events and WebSocket updates retain their existing path.

This follows the production thin-runner rollout and #1067. It adds no new runner, job, status contract, polling loop, or business-work replay.

prs.title: Reuse the API Redis pool for execution control and notifications
prs.body:
## Product Updates

- [x] Other — Workflow control and notifications reuse the API’s Redis pool, avoiding repeated TLS setup on each operation.

## Summary

With TLS-backed Redis, execution control and notifications created, verified, and closed a fresh client for every operation. Production stack samples showed certificate-store loading on the API event loop while ordinary SDK/table traffic saturated its one-core budget; safe workflow bodies took milliseconds but callers waited seconds.

Initialize the existing shared Redis pool in the API lifespan and let `get_redis()` borrow it only on its owning process and event loop. Borrowers preserve the existing error contract and do not close the pool. Short-lived thread/`asyncio.run()` loops retain isolated clients. Serialize initialization, clean failed/cancelled candidates, and close the pool after execution control and pubsub drain. Test teardown now closes both process-global Redis pools on their owning test loop.

Refs #1052.

## Local validation

Before queueing, compare exact current main (`ba9e9ec85ba343265e80e45d62bd1913b148345e`) and this patch in the same Docker stack using verified Redis TLS, the standard CA trust store, a one-core API, and a two-core worker. Four concurrent writers exercise real table batch upserts and notifications. Experimental TLS Compose settings and the load fixture are removed from the change.

| Warm caller median | Main | Patch |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Pure workflow under table-write load | 484 ms | 200 ms |
| SDK-reading workflow under table-write load | 613 ms | 201 ms |
| Pure workflow, quiet | 130 ms | 104 ms |
| SDK-reading workflow, quiet | 159 ms | 135 ms |

The parallel 160-read SDK diagnostic under that load improves from 33.4 to 43.8 reads/s. Every call verifies its result; these local measurements are not a production latency claim.

prs.title: Reduce warmed API memory and dependency overhead
prs.body:
The warmed API retained duplicated AWS service metadata, expanded catalog/OpenAPI graphs, and ORM relationships unrelated to the request. This reduces the matched local working set from 576.7 to 372.2 MiB (392.6 MiB after exercising every document renderer), while keeping the existing API/worker architecture and public contracts.

The change uses a narrow HTTPX S3 transport with AWS CRT signing/checksums, the official MCP SDK's bundled FastMCP, compact catalog/OpenAPI storage, explicit ORM loading, and deferred format libraries. The unused Python pgvector/NumPy dependency is removed; PostgreSQL vector support remains. MCP OAuth/discovery, dynamic tool refresh, scoped execution, and agent-profile manifest serialization have regression coverage.

Validation includes 10,266 backend unit tests; 117 focused transport/artifact/manifest regressions; 20 changed-file integration tests; previous real local runs of all 23 PlatformJob types; and live DigitalOcean Spaces acceptance with both the old SDK and candidate. Python lint/types, production client build/lint/types, all 3,981 client tests, and changed-line CodeQL for both Python and JavaScript pass. The first merge-queue run exposed an encoded-space listing regression in interrupted file-move recovery. The transport now matches the previous SDK’s space/plus decoding; parser and real-storage regression coverage preserve recovery and numbered-path authorization. The merge queue remains the complete E2E/browser/image gate.

Measured local checks took 132.7s versus 136.1s; cached launch-to-ready medians were 8.2s versus 9.9s. These are small local samples. Full catalog enumeration trades about 11–13ms for lower memory, and deferred renderers incur first-use work. Real AWS deployment credential chains/conditional races were not live-tested; production uses DigitalOcean Spaces. The S3 transport is the largest maintenance tradeoff.

Detailed measurements and acceptance evidence: `docs/benchmarks/2026-10-25-api-hosting-memory.md`. Production rollout and safe workflow/webhook comparisons will follow the verified image publication.

A real-Postgres control of 20 warmed fresh-session calls fell from 15 to 10 SQL statements per call, 8.620 to 5.172 ms median, and 152.004 to 95.877 ms total process CPU. These are authentication measurements, not a whole-workflow latency promise. The regression test also verifies subsequent role revocation and user deletion.

Validation: 111 focused runtime/caller/worker-SDK unit tests, 16 integration checks covering scoped SDK access, real agent dispatch/summaries and consent/revocation, API lint/types, and fresh changed-line CodeQL passed. prs.title: Explain app build OOM failures and recovery options
prs.body:
App builds that run out of memory now retain an actionable explanation across App deploys, SDK rebuilds, legacy publishing, and Solution deploy/install/Git sync. Confirmed OOM, preventive memory stops, and unexplained SIGKILL/exit 137 are distinguished; a SIGKILL alone is described as possible OOM.

The shared error recommends increasing build-container memory or using `bifrost solution deploy` to build and deploy prebuilt output locally for non-Git-connected Solutions. The existing durable job, notification/WebSocket, and CLI transports carry the same explanation. SDK packaging failures are covered before Vite starts.

Validation:
- 201 focused backend unit tests passed across classifiers, supervisors, caller propagation, notification projection, and CLI polling.
- `./test.sh tests/e2e/platform/test_app_build_memory_failure.py -v --durations=0`: passed (one real queued App build; Vite config emits a synthetic OOM diagnostic without exhausting memory). 9.53 s call, 3.47 s setup, 0.03 s teardown. This proves the subprocess-to-worker-to-public-error-and-notification boundary; edge cases stay in unit tests.
- `./test.sh quality api`: pyright and Ruff passed.
- Full backend/client/browser suites were not run locally; the merge queue is the complete-suite gate. No frontend or DTO changes.

Product Updates: Other / fix — App build memory failures now explain the cause and how to recover.

Related: #1028 handles ordinary npm/Vite failure output. This change is scoped to memory failures and preserves other error handling.

Release notes

v3.5.0

The "Protected by ALTCHA" footer link can now be reached with the keyboard. Its tabindex="-1" is removed in all built-in translations, so pressing Tab moves from the checkbox to the footer link and then to the next form control. The link's aria-label now also tells screen reader users that it opens in a new tab, for example "Altcha (official website, opens in new tab)".

If you override the footer string with your own translation, nothing changes for you. The widget renders your custom string exactly as you wrote it.

prs.title: Stop preview auth retry storms and worker socket errors
prs.body:
## Summary

A preview left running after its login was revoked repeatedly called the production refresh endpoint. Remember a terminal refresh rejection for that credential generation, return the existing login error locally, and adopt a replacement login without restarting the preview. Keep rate-limit, server, and transport failures recoverable.

Apply the same recovery guard to HTTP and both API WebSocket paths, handle a first upstream WebSocket 401, and remove the auth error page's automatic reload. Worker admission failures also close their socket only once instead of producing a second-close ASGI traceback. Authentication and admission checks remain unchanged.

The included investigation memo records the production allocator attribution and local buffer-burst comparisons. The allocator setting experiment was rolled back after production latency could not be validated; this PR makes no allocator/deployment configuration change.

## Validation

- 82 focused credential, client retry, preview HTTP/WebSocket, and remote-host unit tests passed.
- Real API single-use refresh rotation passed.
- Both existing remote-runner reconnect/cancellation lifecycle tests passed, including a large result and exactly-once side effect.
- API pyright and ruff passed. Earlier manifest contract checks passed (15 tests).
- Read-only final review passed after correcting the WebSocket consumer gap.
- Complete suites were not run locally; the merge queue supplies the full gate.

## Product Updates

- [x] Other — Local previews stop retrying rejected logins and reconnect after a new login; refused worker connections no longer produce duplicate-close errors.
- [ ] Highlight
- [ ] Omit

prs.title: Reduce policy logging work and advance full-pool worker updates
prs.body:
Typed-runtime table and file policy checks reloaded the run-user and workflow facts that authentication had just verified, solely to record the enforced decision. Seed the existing request-local recording cache from verified authority; enforcement, role/revocation checks and post-response persistence remain unchanged. A PostgreSQL control reduced this recording step from six SELECTs / 14.686 ms to zero / 0.156 ms; this is not an end-to-end latency claim.

A full pool of old workers could wait for idle/lifetime retirement before finding a replacement slot. When no replacement is starting, allow only measured ready standard capacity above the warm minimum to drain first. Active work finishes naturally, draining workers still count toward Max Workers, and pools exactly at the warm minimum retain the existing wait. Headroom still launches the replacement first.

Validation: 125 focused tests across collector, policy recording, runtime authority/revocation, HTTP middleware and worker-pool behavior; independent static review. API lint/types passed. Three live-service audit contract checks passed, covering run-user roles, Full workflow authority and secret-value redaction; their shared fixture executes two real workflows. The merge queue remains the complete-suite gate.

The allocator experiment remains rolled back. This change makes no claim of reaching the 250 MiB fully warmed API target; measurements and limits are in `docs/benchmarks/2026-10-26-api-auth-and-allocator.md`.

prs.title: docs: correct production diagnostic impact and warmed baseline
prs.body:
The production benchmark report incorrectly attributed the later CPU drop to completion of a large workload. Native profiling disrupted API readiness, both physical workers lost heartbeats, and 12 running workflows failed through the canonical lost-worker recovery. Record that incident and exclude the subsequent lower-load samples from code-only performance claims.

Also replace the obsolete 250 MiB goal with the user-confirmed ~350 MiB warmed baseline, citing the saved 342/372 MiB working-set observations and their separate PSS values.

Validation: cross-checked the read-only worker/execution audit and prior-night memory artifacts; `git diff --check`. Documentation only; runtime tests were not repeated for this edit. No issue created, per the request to keep the investigation as a spike.

prs.title: Release Redis listener connections when unsubscribe fails
prs.body:
When a Redis cancel or pool-command listener disconnects, a failed unsubscribe currently skips closing the PubSub object and leaves its connection checked out. Always attempt close during cleanup so reconnect cycles release their old connection.

This is a confirmed cleanup defect found during the production memory investigation. Current production pool counters do not show accumulated checked-out connections, so this PR makes no claim to restore the API memory baseline.

Validation: a real Redis regression reproduced the old leak and passes three failure cycles for each listener; all four focused listener tests pass. API pyright and ruff pass. Independent final review found no actionable issues. The merge queue provides the broader suite gate; it was not repeated locally.

Product Updates: Other / Fixed — release Redis listener connections after disconnect cleanup fails.

prs.title: Avoid rebuilding unused workflow tool argument models
prs.body:
Workflow-tool registration generated a Pydantic argument model from every synthetic **arguments wrapper, although dispatch validates the workflow's stored JSON schema directly. Full catalog refreshes rebuilt those unused models. Construct workflow tools with shared SDK metadata and keep each workflow's callable and JSON schema distinct. Native-tool argument validation remains intact.

A local control matching production's 701 workflow tools retained about 43 MiB above baseline after five refreshes and quiet; the shared version retained under 1 MiB. Five rebuilds took 2.11 seconds versus 21.8 milliseconds, with equivalent public tool fields and first-call results. These are local control results; production's warmed memory baseline remains under investigation.

Validation: 27 focused MCP unit tests; the existing live register/list/call integration test, including invalid argument rejection; API pyright and ruff. Broader suites are left to the exact merge-queue candidate.

Product Updates: Other / Fixed — workflow tool updates use less memory and rebuild faster.

## Validation
- Replacement documentation URL returned HTTP 200.

## Product Updates
